#9931. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#9929. Dell and HPE both say they’ve become ‘different companies’

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company.

Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”

HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO said HPE expects better growth ahead, because new server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®

#9928. AWS Weekly Roundup: Local Zone in Bogotá, 30-minute Lambda timeout, and more (November 24, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does. AWS Lambda launched in 2014 with a 60-second timeout, moved to 5 minutes in 2015 and to 15 minutes in 2018, and then stayed there for eight years. Last week the limit doubled, and in the same week Lambda learned to run on GPUs and gave platform teams their own runtimes. That is a lot of Lambda for one week.

Two other threads ran through the week. A new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá brought AWS infrastructure closer to users in Colombia. And AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), Amazon Cognito, and Amazon CloudFront each shipped a piece of identity for agents: who an agent is when it shows up at your door, and how little it should be allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a new Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia. AWS Local Zones place compute, storage, and networking near large metropolitan areas with the same APIs and tools as a Region, for workloads like real-time gaming, live streaming, and financial transactions. The Bogotá Local Zone supports Amazon EC2 C7i, M7i, and R7i instances, Amazon EBS gp3, gp2, and io1 volumes with local snapshots, Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Direct Connect, and Application Load Balancer. To start, enable us-east-1-bog-1a in AWS Global View.

AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute timeout for on-demand Event Functions – You can now configure any Event Function with a timeout of up to 30 minutes (1,800 seconds), double the previous limit, for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also go to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and event source mapping invocations keep the 90-minute timeout from September. Standard Lambda pricing applies, in all commercial Regions. Agentic requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, and file conversion are the workloads AWS calls out. Before raising the value, read the considerations in the Compute blog post: a service that invokes your function synchronously applies its own timeout, client read and socket timeouts need to be longer, and a NAT gateway drops idle connections after 350 seconds, so long calls need keep-alives. For longer work, durable functions still run for up to a year, and now emit OpenTelemetry traces.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances – You can now run GPU-accelerated inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing as Lambda functions, packaged as OCI container images, with no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile. In the walkthrough, four concurrent requests shared one copy of the model on a single GPU and finished in about the same time as one. It’s optimized for inference with custom models, on G-series instances from G4dn to G6e. You pay the EC2 instance fee (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply), a 9.75% management fee for GPU instances, and $0.20 per million requests.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon Polly now supports voice cloning – You can now create a custom voice in Amazon Polly from a few minutes of recordings of a consenting speaker, running on the Polly generative engine. It launches in seven languages, including English, Spanish, and Portuguese, and each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. Polly doesn’t keep the recordings or train on them. Creating a voice is free, and you pay for the speech you synthesize. It’s a gated release, so request access through your account team. The ML blog post covers brand-voice use cases for contact centers, voice agents, and content.

AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes – You can now manage a Lambda runtime as its own resource, separate from function deployment. Platform teams package approved SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring agents as an OCI image in Amazon ECR, and functions pick up updates as Lambda recycles execution environments, with no per-function redeploys. Updates can be staged, with health metrics and rollback. There’s no additional charge, and the Compute blog walkthrough shows the platform-team workflow.

AWS STS announces GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions at runtime – You can now take the temporary credentials a workload already holds and derive narrower ones, cutting permissions, session duration, or both. The result keeps the caller’s original identity, and permissions only ever narrow, so a sub-agent can never end up with more access than whoever created it. Access to the API is controlled with IAM policies, and every call lands in AWS CloudTrail. It’s available in all commercial Regions and beyond, including GovCloud (US) and China.

Amazon Cognito now supports dynamic client registration – You can now let MCP clients and AI agents register themselves at runtime (RFC 7591) instead of creating an app client in advance for each one. You choose between requiring an access token with a registration scope or opening registration to any client, and dynamically registered clients carry a client ID prefix so you can filter and manage them with the rest. It’s available on the Essentials and Plus plans, and client ID metadata documents arrived the same week.

Amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls – You can now call your own APIs from a function with cf.fetch() and act on the response, so authorization, personalization, or fraud checks that used to need Lambda@Edge or a trip to the origin can run at the edge. AWS’s own example: check an AI agent’s permissions and usage budget before the request reaches your API or MCP server. Network calls cost $0.10 per million on top of invocation charges and are included in the Pro flat-rate plan and above. The Networking blog post also covers cf.beacon() for background analytics.

Amazon Aurora DSQL now supports multi-Region peering across continents – You can now build a multi-Region Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster with peers on different continents, such as US East (N. Virginia) and Europe (Ireland), and read and write to one strongly consistent database from both. It was a busy week for DSQL: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures arrived, and storage upgrades brought up to 50% higher write throughput at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers – With more than 12,500 developers in R&D, BMW treats governance as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop, mostly in the CI/CD pipeline, so neither the agent nor its prompts can override it.

AI coding agents on Amazon EC2 Mac: How Cognition scales Devin for macOS – Cognition starts a fresh macOS VM for each Devin session in under a minute on Amazon EC2 Mac hosts across six Regions. The detail worth stealing: sessions are decoupled from hosts, and Cognition reports that about 90% release their VM when idle and resume from a snapshot in seconds.

How Klaviyo processes 3 billion daily events at scale with Amazon MSK Express – Timely reading for Black Friday week. Klaviyo moved from RabbitMQ to Amazon MSK Express brokers to absorb roughly 7 times normal event volume during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Running one set of processors across three priority topics, instead of separate infrastructure per level, cut costs by roughly 30%, according to the team.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – It’s next week: join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, or register for the free livestream to follow the keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

#9925. Nutanix CEO announces gradual departure, intent to complete set of storage links

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until new hire lands, then stick around as advisor

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole new set of ecosystems.”

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO said the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix announced its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami said high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®

#9923. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from the first quarter and 39% from the second, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's "The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026" report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gangs, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9922. This could mess with Thanksgiving, says VMware as it drops third critical patch bundle in a week

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues.

VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the new advisory includes the following remarks:

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

Two of the other critical flaws in this new advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that users can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

In past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®

#9919. Jury finds Huawei stole US tech, laundered money, and broke sanctions

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

This case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision says Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors showed evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”

Another item of evidence apparently showed a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a company called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ says.

The feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®

#9915. Government may apply TV license fee to streaming services to fund the BBC

Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year

A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its plans for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.

One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

As any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

The government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," said NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere says more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading.  Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

"Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo."

Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.

Current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

#9912. Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.

Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.

Project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, currently follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug. This will no longer be the case. As of the announcement on Nov. 13, Google changed its policy to disclose 90 days after reporting to the vendor. As of Feb. 2, 2027, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 60 days. As of Jan. 3, 2028, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 30 days.

In a blog post outlining the decision, Google's Natalie Silvanovich wrote that while the intention of 90+30 was to encourage faster patching while giving vendors time to deliver patches, "The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient."

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

Specifically, Silvanovich noted that large language models have enabled threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster in today's AI era.

"A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster," she wrote. "LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior."

Project Zero is not a conventional bug disclosure program. Founded in 2014, the organization was established specifically so Google could help facilitate the safe reporting and disclosure of high-severity, high-impact vulnerabilities found in widely used software and hardware. That said, Project Zero's move reflects a broad inundation of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and where Google goes, the rest of the industry may follow.

As for whether such a thing is good, bad, or necessary for the cybersecurity industry, experts appear to be split.

Disclosure timelines are a key part of the vulnerability ecosystem. When a researcher or firm discovers a vulnerability and submits it to the software developer responsible, a standard timeline is usually designated for the developer to fix the vulnerability; such deadlines are usually 90 or 120 days, but it varies depending on the bug, disclosure policy, and circumstances.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

If the software developer ignores the bug report, is slow to address it, or declines to communicate with the researcher, the researcher may choose to disclose the flaw at the end of the disclosure timeline to inform security teams and practitioners of the looming threat. These timelines hold software vendors accountable and encourage them to maintain secure software, but it's not perfect science.

Oftentimes, the researcher and software developer will work together to coordinate a disclosure date so relevant research, patches, and mitigations are ready at the same time. Sometimes, if the bug is especially dangerous or requires more time to fix, the timeline may change and the technical details and proof-of-concept exploits will be held until a later date.

It's worth noting there are no standard requirements between platforms. HackerOne keeps its default disclosure timeline to 30 days, though it's broadly set at the program level by each vendor customer, and many HackerOne programs set longer timelines. Bugcrowd researchers and vendors generally coordinate timelines; program rules again supersede standards.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative (which is not a platform but a vendor-agnostic vulnerability disclosure program) uses a standard disclosure timeline of 120 days for responsive vendors that release working patches, and shorter timelines for vulnerabilities that result from faulty patches.

It remains to be seen whether the larger industry will follow Project Zero's lead. Dustin Childs, ZDI's head of threat awareness, calls Google's decision "a bold move to be sure, especially considering the explosion of bug reports coming in thanks to AI assisted discovery."

However, he worries about how shorter timelines may impact remediation quality. "I fear it will lead to patches that don’t fully address the vulnerability. We see that happen at 120 days," Childs says. "We’ll be watching closely to see how this change impacts vendors and researchers alike."

Alex Rice, cofounder, CISO, and CTO at HackerOne, tells Dark Reading that he expects the industry to move in Google's direction, though not necessarily in lockstep. He argues that patch soak time no longer protects defenders, given how quickly attackers can exploit flaws now. And because Project Zero is a disclosure program for vulnerabilities with demonstrated impact and not a bug bounty platform that addresses a broad range of flaws, Google is in a unique position to set aggressive expectations.

"The specifics will still vary by program, severity, and whether a fix is realistic, and platforms like ours will need to support that flexibility," Rice says. "But the direction isn’t in question. Organizations should plan for 30 days as the baseline expectation that will shrink even further."

Between stories from this year about AI models capable of discovering zero-day bugs off of human language prompts and vulnerability coordinators fighting huge spikes in bug reporting volumes the past couple of years, Google's position seems defensible. The tech giant isn't alone in its move either: In January, Anthropic's own coordinated disclosure policy will shorten from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity bugs, and 45 days for all other cases.

But not everyone agrees. Expel principal threat researcher Marcus Hutchins took issue with the move in a post to X, where he noted that 2026 has already seen far more CVEs than 2025. "Sure, there are some vendors who just sit on bugs forever and don't make any effort to patch them. But there's way more overworked & underpaid teams, non-profits, and solo projects who are patching bugs as fast as they physically can," he wrote.

Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security and a pioneer in vulnerability disclosure, largely agrees. As she tells Dark Reading, even AI firms currently struggle to patch the issues they find, leaving volunteers and less resourced firms even further back against the wall. "A deadline doesn't magically manifest a fix."

"Researchers and AI companies are burying maintainers in bug reports and not doing enough to help fix them. This isn't even a matter of model access or token cost. The AI companies themselves can't even close the gap," she says. "Anthropic reports that 629 of the 5,087 vulnerabilities it disclosed have been patched. OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, run with security engineers from Trail of Bits, has written patches for a third of the 2,055 issues it found, and 23% have been accepted upstream."

[Editor's Note: After publication, a Trail of Bits spokesperson told Dark Reading that of the most recent finding of 2,162 issues found, 733 have a patch written, and among those, 506 (or about 69%) have been accepted or merged upstream.]

A Google spokesperson tells Dark Reading that in creating the new policy, the company solicited feedback from the vendors Project Zero reports the most vulnerabilities to, including open source projects.

"The general consensus was that these timelines are achievable, and most open source projects are almost there," the spokesperson says. "Every vulnerability that Project Zero reported against a volunteer-maintained project in 2026 was fixed in 30 days, except for one, which was fixed in 31 days. Open source projects are among the vendors who will need to make the fewest changes to meet our new policy, as they are already doing so well."

While one side of the argument disagrees with the rollout of shorter timelines, the other side sees it as inevitable or necessary to respond to how attackers now use AI to pursue their goals. HackerOne's Rice says that right now, teams are not ready to deal with a 30-day turnaround, but Google's move may offer an opportunity at the boardroom level to convince technology and executive partners that remediation is a shared responsibility.

"If you're a security team struggling to keep up, don't waste time playing the victim. Take this as a gift," he says. "Ask for dedicated engineering capacity for security fixes, pre-agreed remediation SLAs, automated validation and retesting, and the authority to ship mitigations while the full fix is built. The teams that turn this pressure into that conversation will be far ahead of the ones hoping for external relief."

Casey Ellis, founder of Bugcrowd and The disclose.io Project, says this is a necessary evolution, even if it feels aggressive. In the wake of proliferated vulnerability discovery, the timeline shortening "puts productive pressure on response and fix pipelines."

Ellis says he feels the typical targets of Project Zero researchers are in "decent shape," but community norms tend to follow Google's lead on CVE timelines, so the move could carry larger impact.

"My main concern would be companies that maintain safety-critical systems or those that are otherwise logistically difficult to update; a security fix doesn't always end with a patch, and more often than not, it doesn't," he says. "The Project Zero changes will ultimately reveal (and hopefully shrink or close) the readiness gap for many PSIRT teams, products, and hosted service providers, but unless product vendors become proactive about this aspect of vulnerability discovery and disclosure it is likely to be a bumpy ride for some."

This story was updated on Nov. 18, 2026 at 8:47 a.m. ET, with additional context shared by a Trail of Bits spokesperson regarding figures included in the article.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. #9911. Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Two AI agents, separately over a five-day period, autonomously tried to access connected applications, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, and GitHub, without account owner permission.

Grok Bots attempted to access corporate applications without their users' approval or knowledge, presenting yet another security challenge for enterprises as AI agents become increasingly autonomous.

Researchers at NewCore identified 31 unprompted attempts by two xAI Grok Bots to access connected corporate applications over a five-day period, including Google Calendar, Gmail, Slack, GitHub, and Notion, according to the findings of an investigation published today. In one case, the bot continued making background requests even after its owner had declined offers for recurring check-ins four times.

The requests were not approved and did not reach the underlying corporate data: NewCore had placed a security gateway between the agents and the applications, requiring human approval for each request.

"Over five days, two Grok Bots on NewCore employee accounts made 31 requests to calendar, email, Slack, GitHub and Notion while nobody was talking to them, some with the laptop shut," Ido Hoorvitch, security research team lead at NewCore, wrote in the report.

Related:Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

One bot repeatedly attempted to retrieve Google Calendar events in the evening, overnight, and the following day, despite there being no active conversation with its owner. In a second case, another bot attempted to access Notion's calendar tools before Google Calendar had even been connected. It continued making requests while its owner's laptop was closed and asleep.

The investigation began as an internal experiment at NewCore, which wanted to understand how autonomous AI agents behave when connected to real corporate systems. The company earlier this year provided employees with enterprise Grok Bot accounts and connected the agents to corporate services, including email, calendars, Notion, and other business applications.

However, NewCore put a handbrake in place: It did not give the agents unrestricted, standing access to company data. Instead, requests had to pass through its Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway. The gateway sent an approval notification to the employee who owned the account whenever a Grok Bot tried to access an application. If a request was not approved within three minutes, it automatically expired and was denied, Hoorvitch said.

"We did it because we had no way to audit why an agent reaches for data, and until we do, the gate stays closed by default," he wrote. Ultimately, this security control allowed NewCore to observe and reconstruct the bots' background activity.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

The first sign that something was amiss came after an employee used Grok Bot to retrieve their daily calendar, approving the request through the gateway as expected. Later that evening, however, the gateway recorded further calendar access attempts, despite the employee no longer interacting with the bot.

This led investigators to uncover repeated attempts by Grok agents to access corporate applications without any corresponding user interaction. Moreover, when one bot was asked whether it had made the gateway calls, it said it had not, Hoorvitch said. The requests did not appear in the bot's chat history.

"It was telling the truth. … That is the part to sit with," he wrote. "An agent that cannot account for its own actions is not a bug report. It is a finding."

NewCore contacted xAI about its findings and said the company's support team confirmed that the activity was not the result of a software vulnerability or an exploit, but was part of Grok Bot's built-in background check-in functionality.

"These are built-in background check-ins by the primary bot, during a check-in the bot looks at its connected sources, and there is no user or admin setting to turn them off," Hoorvitch wrote, relaying the response from xAI support.

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

According to NewCore, xAI also said that customers seeking to stop the check-ins could send the vendor a list of employee sign-in addresses. NewCore said it had not received an official response from xAI's media team at the time the report was published.

The lack of a user- or administrator-facing setting to disable background check-ins, or to control which connected tools they can use, creates a visibility and governance challenge for security teams. Employees may not know when an AI agent is accessing connected applications, while the agent itself may not retain a record of its server-initiated activity in the chat history visible to its owner.

"The danger is not that the model goes rogue," Hoorvitch explains to Dark Reading. "The concern is that we hand agents standing credentials and then let someone else decide when they act. The owner thinks the bot works when they talk to it. The vendor thinks a helpful bot checks in on its own. The model does what the platform tells it in that turn, not what the owner would have said."

Though "nobody in that chain is malicious," he says, "the result is still a bot reading your inbox at 7:46 a.m. while you are asleep."

The distinction matters because all 31 unattended requests identified by NewCore were read operations, such as retrieving calendar events or searching messages, Hoorvitch explains. None resulted in data being accessed, because the gateway blocked them. However, the same connected tool sets included capabilities to take actions, such as sending email, modifying calendar events, and posting Slack messages. NewCore warned that the same background processes could pose a greater risk if they were to invoke those write-capable tools.

In NewCore's investigation, its MCP gateway blocked all 31 unattended requests. The company argues that organizations need similar independent controls to set and enforce policies on AI agents operating within their systems.

"Put the decision outside the agent," Hoorvitch says. "Route every agent tool call through something you own, like the NewCore MCP Gateway, where the owner's policy decides what goes through and every call is logged whether or not the agent remembers it."

NewCore also recommends that organizations immediately inventory the agents connected to corporate tools, identify which applications and data they can reach, and assign an owner to each. Security teams should review not only approved activity but also requests that were denied or left unanswered, since these can reveal what agents attempt to do without user involvement.

"Most teams cannot answer that today," Hoorvitch says, "and you cannot govern what you cannot list."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9909. The world's fastest computers have a problem: Keeping the work running

I node what you did last summer: you went down when an HPC project was relying on you

Frontier, Oak Ridge National Laboratory's exascale supercomputer, has thousands of processors working together on scientific problems. It also has a surprisingly ordinary way of ruining a researcher's day: one node going down.

An uncorrectable memory error can do it, or a maintenance mishap. Scott Atchley, chief technology officer at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, describes technicians accidentally rebooting the wrong node or risking a neighboring node's power supply while working in tightly packed racks.

The hardware fault can affect just one node, but a simulation running across thousands of processors can grind to a halt. Then comes a series of questions. How recently did the application save its progress? How much computation needs repeating? And how long before the scheduler lets the job run again?

For operators, the challenge isn't just keeping the supercomputer running. It's keeping the science moving.

On Frontier, a memory error can have an outsized audience. Atchley says uncorrectable double-bit errors in high-bandwidth memory occurred about 1.5 times a day during the supercomputer's early bring-up.

Its predecessor, Summit, saw roughly one every two weeks. This sounds like a backward step, until you count the memory. Frontier has more than 16 times as much, giving bad bits considerably more places to hide.

Memory isn't the only problem. Problematic GPU firmware can crash a node, and so can a technician rebooting the wrong one. Interconnect faults add another way for a large job to come unstuck.

In a tightly coupled simulation using the Message Passing Interface (MPI) simulation, thousands of processes, or ranks, exchange data and participate in collective operations. If one rank disappears, the others cannot carry on as though nothing happened.

Clockwork.io CEO Suresh Vasudevan describes a similar dependency in synchronized GPU training.

One failed GPU can bring a 1,024-GPU job to a pause. An underperforming GPU can be almost as troublesome: if one participant runs at 80 percent speed, others might have to spend time waiting for it.

The bigger the machine, the more ways there are for one small problem to become everybody's problem.

Since stopping every component from failing isn't an option, researchers need a way to preserve their work. That's where checkpointing comes in. The application periodically saves its state so that, when something goes wrong, the simulation can resume from an earlier point instead of starting from scratch.

The catch is that saving progress costs computing time, and doing it too often can become almost as wasteful as losing the work itself.

Vasudevan explains this with an example. If writing a checkpoint takes 30 seconds, saving every five minutes consumes roughly 10 percent of computing time. Stretch that interval to 50 minutes, and the overhead drops to about 1 percent. But a failure could wipe out considerably more work.

Atchley says the calculation depends on the job's size and expected failure rate. He uses an example of ten-hour mean time between failures for a full machine job on Frontier. Using half the machine would roughly double that interval. The Young-Daly checkpointing model helps find the balance between saving too frequently and risking too much work.

Researchers also have the scheduler to contend with. Frontier's standard batch queue limits larger jobs to 12 hours, with shorter limits for smaller jobs. Its extended queue permits jobs of up to 64 nodes to run for 24 hours.

Then there's storage. Checkpoints can be written to the Lustre-based Orion filesystem or node-local SSDs. The faster the data can be saved, the less time checkpointing steals from the actual science.

Before recovery can begin, someone has to notice the job has stalled. Vasudevan says frameworks such as PyTorch can spend several minutes waiting before a hung process is recognized. Operators then have to sift through application logs and hardware telemetry to try to identify the offending GPU.

This can mean another encounter with the scheduler, which decides when replacement resources become available. Once allocated, the application still needs to load its libraries, initialize the runtime, and rebuild communication connections between processors.

And that's before the lost work enters the picture.

Restarting from a checkpoint means returning to the last saved state, potentially hours earlier, and repeating every calculation that has been completed since. The hardware may be back in action, but the simulation hasn't caught up.

Atchley says Frontier can launch a scheduled job in roughly 30 seconds. Restoring the application's data and getting back to useful computation takes longer.

Worse, researchers who lose their allocation may have to rejoin the queue. Depending on demand, Atchley says, "it might take me a day or so before my job runs again."

Keeping a supercomputer available is one thing. Making sure its processors are doing useful work is another, and the difference is measurable.

A 2026 study by researchers Carlo Graziani, Bethany Lusch, and Bronson Messer examined computational efficiency using records of 331,640 jobs run on Frontier during 2024. Their model estimated that, even with optimally timed checkpoints, only 95.7 percent of allocated computing resources would go toward useful calculations.

The remaining 4.3 percent? Around 1.2 percent goes to writing checkpoints, 2.8 percent disappears into failures, and another 0.3 percent is spent restarting applications.

Skipping checkpoints altogether would be worse. The model puts useful computation at just 91.4 percent without proactive checkpointing, demonstrating that saving work has a cost, but losing it can cost considerably more.

These efficiency figures are modeled estimates, not measurements of every source of lost productivity. They don't capture every delay from rejoining queues, stalled applications, or poorly performing components. The actual productivity bill can be harder to pin down.

This makes Frontier's reported 98.49 percent overall availability in 2024 an interesting contrast. The Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility's operational assessment measures how often the system was available to users.

Scale makes these losses expensive. An hour of wasted computation across 2,000 nodes represents 2,000 node hours gone, compared with just 100 node hours for a job using 100 nodes.

Saving checkpoints to local SSDs can speed things up, but there's a catch. If the node fails, the checkpoint stored on it can disappear too.

Atchley points to techniques such as Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's Scalable Checkpoint/Restart (SCR), which can copy checkpoint data to neighboring nodes. This gives applications another recovery point if the original node goes down.

Keeping spare nodes available can also shorten recovery time. Atchley says researchers who reserve extra nodes will consume their computing allocation even if nothing breaks, which leaves fewer hours for useful computation.

Software developers are also trying to avoid the restart process altogether. Vasudevan describes techniques that attempt to transfer distributed application state to replacement hardware to allow synchronized workloads to continue without returning to an earlier checkpoint.

Some approaches can handle certain GPU and network failures through failover. These techniques depend on detecting faults quickly, preserving consistent application state, and having replacement resources available.

None of this makes failures disappear. Atchley notes that hardware improvements, including stronger memory protection, can address problems encountered on earlier machines. But as systems grow, new failure modes emerge.

The next generation of supercomputers may fix the faults that plagued their predecessors, but that doesn't mean they'll never break. Atchley explains that problems solved on one machine tend to give way to entirely new ones on the next.

Faster processors and more memory are only useful if scientists can keep their calculations moving. This makes fault detection and recovery every bit as important as another headline-grabbing performance record.

Resilience research, Atchley admits, "is not sexy at all." But when you're dealing with machines of this size, "scale just amplifies everything." ®
