#9864. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9862. HP sees premium-priced AI PCs as its meal ticket in a shrinking market

PC shipments set to fall further thanks to the memory shortage, but high-margin models for AI at the edge keep profits up

HP Inc expects the PC market to shrink by "high single to low double digits" in calendar 2027, squeezed by the memory chip crisis, but execs reckon the corporation can still gain share by focusing on premium categories and AI PCs.

Interim CEO Bruce Broussard said HP would do this "by capitalizing on the growing shift of AI workloads to the edge and leveraging our industry-leading portfolio designed to meet the needs of users with more demanding workloads."

The pitch echoes the previous quarter's earnings call. "Our focus is on helping customers implement and manage AI across their environments. We believe that the future of AI is hybrid with workloads running both in the cloud and closer to where people work and data is created," he added.

Broussard cited IDC estimates that half of enterprise AI inference workloads will run on endpoints or edge nodes by 2030, and claimed that with half a billion devices shipped, HP has "deep expertise in how devices perform, how they're secured and how they're managed at scale."

HP fourth quarter revenue - for the three months ended October 31 - was $16 billion, up 9.3 percent year-on-year. Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue was up 9.5 percent to $60 billion. Personal Systems drove the growth, as its printer business slipped slightly.

Personal Systems revenue grew 14 percent on commercial and advanced compute sales, and AI PCs represented nearly 60 percent of HP’s shipments in the quarter.

"That said, higher component costs and challenging pricing environment, particularly in consumer, pressured profitability," said Broussard.

Like its rivals, HP is leaning on higher-margin premium models and signing long-term deals with the memory chip makers to secure supplies. Nikkei Asia named HP among the firms buying a limited amount of memory from China’s ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT).

Asked whether it planned to procure more Chinese chippery, HP’s CFO Karen Parkhill sidestepped the question: "We don't expect any material changes in our suppliers right now. We're confident in the suppliers that we have, and we are confident in the supply that we have what we need to fulfil the demand this year."

She conceded that "We are using suppliers from all over the world."

Parkhill said HP expects memory and storage costs to continue rising, but at a slower rate than during this last fiscal year. "We also expect CPU costs to increase, but not as much as what we've seen with memory and storage. And all of that is baked into our outlook."

Broussard expects Q4 to prove the low point for Personal Systems margins, with improvement coming from further optimization of its product design and component configurations.

In Ferbruary, HP said memory and storage costs had grown from 15 to 18 percent of the PC bill of materials at the start of the year to a figure closer to 40 percent. Parkhill declined to update the figure, saying the moderating cost curves and fast-changing production mix make the BOM percentage "less useful."

HP’s newly hired CEO, former GSK boss Emma Walmsley, will start work at the company on January 4, leading it through what continues to be uncertain times for the PC industry. ®

Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.

In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework.

I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.

This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:

“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”

“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”

In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.

GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground

With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.

With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.

Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.

As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.

The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file.

Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:

“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”

“I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.”

The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own.

Watch John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session 👇

#9857. Microsoft's NTLM security changes trip up third-party logins

It's not our fault if you've implemented it wrong

Microsoft's November security updates can break authentication in some third-party applications and devices following changes to NTLM message signing.

Affected systems include authentication proxy servers, single sign-on (SSO) products, and application packaging tools, the company's support notice says.

The failures stem from products that claim to supply required information during NTLM authentication but return incomplete or empty data, Microsoft said: "An affected device might set the NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE_TARGET_INFO flag in its CHALLENGE_MESSAGE but provide an empty or incomplete TargetInfo field."

Administrators can use the notice's network trace and event log examples to identify affected products. For confirmed cases, the temporary workaround is to set the ClientAllowUnsignedNtlm Registry value to 1 on affected clients. This stops the client offering signing, backing out the new default rather than fixing the incompatible product. The recommended long-term options are a vendor update or Kerberos authentication, where supported.

The value sits under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\MSV1_0 and defaults to 0, enabling clients to offer signing on non-anonymous connections.

The NTLM changes arrived in the November 10 update as phase 1 in a 2-phase process. In phase 1, "Windows client devices begin offering NTLM signing on all connections by default. Servers accept both signed and unsigned clients. Auditing events identify clients not using signing."

Phase 2, scheduled for May 2027, will make Windows servers require NTLM signing by default. "Clients that do not offer signing will be rejected by secure servers," Microsoft stated.

Ominously, Microsoft warned that it "might remove the registry keys at a future date," so the company is not kidding about the temporary workaround thing.

The additional protections were added to address CVE-2026-118737, a vulnerability in which "improper verification of cryptographic signature in Windows Remote Procedure Call Runtime allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network."

NTLM is on Microsoft's hit list, having joined the Deprecated Features list in 2024. It dates back to the era of Windows NT, and Microsoft has made clear that it wants customers to move to Kerberos, which became the default in 2000. Even so, NTLM lingers on.

Deprecation doesn't remove Microsoft's obligation to secure NTLM while it remains in supported Windows releases. For administrators, though, the immediate task is identifying incompatible products before temporary exceptions give way to stricter enforcement. ®

#9854. Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized dent in asteroid Dimorphos

Next step is to move in for a closer look at the carnage

The European Space Agency's Hera probe has revealed a stadium-sized crater on Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA struck with its DART spacecraft in 2022.

The Double Asteroid Redirection Test was deliberately crashed into the asteroid on September 26, 2022. The original plan called for a European spacecraft – Asteroid Impact Mission (AIM) – to launch first and observe the before and after effects of DART. AIM was canceled, and the Hera mission launched in 2024.

DART was a success. Scientists were able to determine that the impact had indeed changed the orbit of Dimorphos. The question was what else had happened to the asteroid. Scientists spotted ejecta and debris following the DART impact, but the close-up observations by Hera have revealed the full extent of the collision.

Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, said: "Scientists debated whether Dimorphos had sustained an impact crater, changed its shape or stayed the same.

"Much to our surprise the answer turns out to be all three at once! The face struck by DART has been flattened into an impact crater the size of a sports stadium, which extends across the asteroid's entire width."

Scientists also noted that the asteroid is now tumbling in its orbit.

Hera is surveying the 151-meter-wide Dimorphos and its larger companion, the 730-meter-wide Didymos, from about 25 to 30 km away. It moves around the pair at roughly 12 cm/s, using thruster firings to trace rectangular paths rather than conventional circular orbits.

The plan is to approach closer, to about 13 km, to get higher-resolution snaps. A complicating factor is the discovery that hundreds of orbiting boulders surround the asteroids. Michael Kueppers, ESA's Hera mission scientist, said: "The team will have to take account of these objects in the coming weeks as the mission moves in closer."

Hera will deploy two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in early 2027. The Italian-led Milani will study surface composition and surrounding dust, while the Luxembourg-led Juventas will use radar to probe Dimorphos's interior before attempting a landing.

Scientists also want to measure Dimorphos's mass. Combined with the observed change in its orbit, that will help them assess how effectively DART transferred momentum to the asteroid and improve predictions for future deflection attempts.

Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli said: "NASA's DART mission demonstrated that we can change an asteroid's orbit. Hera is now revealing what happened to the asteroid itself. By combining these two missions, humanity is taking a decisive step towards making asteroid deflection a reliable tool for protecting our planet." ®

#9853. 1Password Breach Leaked Customer Names and Emails, But Passwords Are Safe

The Fine Print: The following comments are owned by whoever posted them. We are not responsible for them in any way.

Given past experience, perhaps we should wait a few weeks or even months before declaring this as a victory.

The initial announcement of these breaches ALWAYS states that "passwords were not compromised". The company's use of zero-knowledge encryption is important but not sufficient in and of itself. What if, for instance, it turns out the hackers gained sufficient control over 1Password's systems to push a compromised version of the client software out?

are they fucking paying you? The self hosted ecosystem is well-developed and feature rich. There's absolutely no reason to put shit like this on someone else's computer and be at the mercy of their dumbest engineer.

How is clicking paste password a difficult step?

Don't you know that you can self-host Bitwarden? With all the bells and whistles on the client side, as you'll use the official Bitwarden clients?

Keepass does have native mobile support, I use it extensively. In fact you have a choice of Keepass apps on Android. I use KeepassDX.

Maybe you were looking for an "official" Keepass Android app, but that's now how it works. There is a reference implementation, but all the apps are open source and there are multiple on most platforms. Choose the one that suits your needs.

The main benefit of Keepass over things like 1Password is that because it's completely free and you can use free cloud storage if you need

Actually, Keepass2Android [google.com] is available for (obviously) Android. And probably for iToys as well.

Yes: It works off a local file - which is fine. You can either put it in your google drive (yuck!) or use e.g. SyncThing [syncthing.net] (also available for Android) to keep the same file in sync across multiple devices. I find it works nicely with Linux, where I use KeepassXC [keepassxc.org] - and they use the "same" file - actually: a file which SyncThing keeps in sync across devices.

It's true that they only have one job, but it also happens to be the one job that AI is currently skull-fucking. I'm prepared to cut them some slack.

Their 1 job also paints a *huge* target on their backs. Still, I don't know that my passwords will actually be safe there...

The subscription and cloud services came practically together, and then the bloated desktop app using Electron(?)

Pity. I don't mind paying for upgrades but subscriptions got me off 1P. Being Mac only helps.

We keep seeing these news stories about 1Password and others being hacked. So far, not a single browser password manager has been breached. How do they do it? I'm thinking the browser is an underrated and unappreciated hero, when it comes to password security!

I would like an explanation why this employee's account gave access to both the codebase (so, engineer?) and also to the customer database.

I don't follow. Where does a browser password manager fit into your comment?

after gaining access to an employee's corporate GitHub account and pushing malicious code to company servers. The attacker stole customer names, email addresses, account creation dates

So the employee's corporate GitHub account allowed access to code AND customer data. Coders shouldn't have access to customer data.

And what exactly does that have to do with web browser password managers?

Yes, yes they do. When you sign in to Chrome (or any browser), your passwords are synced to every browser you log in to, and also to your phone. They absolutely are in the cloud, stored in your account.

You decide if you want this or not. If you decide to sync them, you're accepting the risk of the provider being hacked, no matter if it is a third-party like 1password or Browser vendor like Mozilla, Google, Opera, etc.

There may be more comments in this discussion. Without JavaScript enabled, you might want to turn on Classic Discussion System in your preferences instead.

#9849. Huawei and crew tout homegrown EDA tools to overcome China’s fab deficit

Chip design software leans heavily into 3D packaging and multi-node assemblies

Chinese telecom and IT giant Huawei boasted about its advancements in domestic electronic design automation (EDA) software this week, which it needs to accelerate the adoption of homegrown chip manufacturing.

EDA is an umbrella term for software, hardware, and services essential to the planning, design, and production of modern chips.

Today, Cadence Design Systems, Synopsys, and Siemens dominate the industry, but US export controls have restricted Huawei and other blacklisted Chinese businesses' access to their tools.

The US blacklisted Huawei back in 2019 over concerns the telecommunications equipment giant could be forced to inject backdoors into its gear.

Unable to access top EDA tools, Huawei’s chip division, HiSilicon, was forced to develop its own with the help of Phlexing Technology.

This week, Phlexing chairman Qing He detailed the company’s efforts to bring new EDA tools to support Huawei’s so-called Tau Scaling Law design philosophy.

“Tau EDA is the domestic EDA tool chain for Tau chips. It comes from a long, close partnership with Huawei,” he said.

We discussed the tech earlier this year, but in a nutshell, it involves using advanced packaging, specifically 3D hybrid bonding, to achieve higher transistor density for a given area.

The TSMC of China, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is still years behind Taiwan, South Korea, and the US on process technology. It currently has the ability to mass-produce chips on the equivalent of a 7 nm process.

For comparison, TSMC began producing 5 nm-class products in 2020 and commenced mass production of 2 nm-class chips in late 2025.

So, Huawei aims to use 3D packaging to close the gap, but for this to happen, it first needs tools capable of designing such chips, and that’s just what Phlexing claims to have done with its GloryBolt and GloryEX platforms.

“Traditional EDA has long handled only single processes. Tau EDA needs to integrate and decompose multiple processes,” He said. “Coupling multi-scale, multi-structure, and multi-physics issues called for new analysis tools.”

This, He says, culminated in the co-development of a process design kit (PDK) with Huawei beginning in 2024. These technologies have now gone live.

The development comes as Huawei looks to bring larger, more capable processors to market.

We previously discussed the company’s latest developments around AI accelerators, near packaged optics, networking, and rack systems. Many of these advancements will depend on multi-die chip packages, enabled by EDA tools, like those built by Phlexing. ®

#9848. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill.

A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary.

I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable.

This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system.

The label on an application rarely tells you enough. “Java microservices” doesn’t tell you which Java Development Kit (JDK) runs in production, where that version is pinned, whether the tests execute, or which interfaces other systems depend on. “Legacy monolith” doesn’t tell you whether the business core is broken or whether one retired platform dependency prevents the application from starting.

Before you recommend a change, build a small evidence inventory:

Record uncertainty while you work. I use three simple labels: documented, inferred, and unverified. If two files disagree about the Java version, resolve the contradiction. If you can’t determine whether a CI check blocks merges, say so. Record the unknown rather than treating a guess as a finding.

That inventory gives you something concrete to review with the people who own the application before you propose changes.

Once you understand the application, make the decision per component. A single system can contain code that should stay, dependencies that should be swapped, and one subsystem that genuinely needs a rewrite.

First, check whether a capability is still needed. Remove it only after verifying that it is unused or superseded and confirming that decision with its owner. Removal is a separate decision, and it’s not necessarily the most disruptive one.

For a capability you still need, start with the option that changes the least:

This is a decision order, not a universal ranking of effort or risk. Ask what evidence justifies choosing a more disruptive option. “The code is old” is not enough. A known vulnerability with no patched release for the pinned version, a dependency that fails on the required runtime, or a measured reliability target the current design cannot meet can justify escalation.

The next question is whether the component can run well enough to produce evidence, even if the legacy CI pipeline is not green.

Run a time-boxed feasibility check. Try to install dependencies, build on an available toolchain, start the component, and execute at least one meaningful test. Stop when the time box expires. The result sends you down one of two paths.

Capture behavior, then upgrade. Use this path when the old application can still run at an acceptable cost. Record its externally visible behavior, fix the test harness where practical, and use those checks to verify the upgrade.

Build a small modern slice first. Use this path when the old component cannot run until you have already changed it. Move the thinnest useful workflow to supported technology, prove it, and expand from there. Requiring a complete legacy test suite in this situation is circular. Restoring the test suite is part of the modernization.

I use the following safety levels, adapted from the doc-and-modernize skill, to describe the strongest regression protection available:

State what you can prove and what risk remains. Even an L4 gate cannot establish that every possible behavior is correct. APIs, database effects, files, rendered output, and business workflows often make durable comparison points because those behaviors can survive a framework or language change.

PiggyMetrics was the clearest example of an application that looked worse than it was. The project used Java 8, Spring Boot 2.0.3, Spring Cloud Finchley, Zuul, Hystrix, and the old spring-security-oauth2 library.

It would have been easy to call the application unworkable and start drawing a new architecture. The feasibility check told a different story.

The recorded feasibility results show these two probes against the legacy checkout with JDK 8:

These are historical results, not commands expected to reproduce those failures on the modernized checkout. The nine errors traced through Failed to load ApplicationContext to an embedded MongoDB download returning HTTP 403. The pinned binary also targeted i386, which would not run on the Apple Silicon host.

The probes did not establish that the whole application ran or that its integration behavior was correct. They did give me a narrower next step: replace the test dependency and rerun the affected tests before changing the production stack.

That result saved me from making a very tidy, very expensive mistake. I had already started thinking about which parts of the architecture I might replace. One broken test dependency did not justify redesigning the application, and five passing tests established behavior I could check for unintended changes during modernization.

The modernization plan turned that evidence into a capture-then-upgrade sequence:

The first acceptance gate was a passing baseline on the old stack, not merely the successful installation of a replacement dependency. Running checks in CI and enforcing them as merge requirements were also separate steps in the plan.

The result summary records the Java and Spring upgrades while retaining the microservice decomposition that the application exists to demonstrate. Eureka and Cloud Config stayed; the two monitoring modules used by the retired Hystrix and Turbine stack were removed. The in-scope build went from nine modules to seven.

Those versions describe the experiment, not a recommendation to select the same versions today. Choose targets against your current support requirements. The useful lesson is how the repository evidence narrowed the change.

The same process produced different answers on two smaller applications. Their pinned reports describe these choices:

The comparison needs one important qualification: DOOM’s checks froze outputs from the modernized engine itself. They protected against later regressions; they did not independently prove parity with a period-correct legacy binary. Naming that limit is part of choosing an honest safety level.

I then applied the method to ADempiere, a large Java suite covering ERP, customer relationship management, manufacturing, supply chain, accounting, and point of sale.

The scale changed the controls, but not the method. The work established a reproducible build, moved the runtime to JDK 21, preserved SOAP web-service contracts while replacing XFire with CXF and Jakarta, captured legacy web behavior, and introduced a modern web path for selected users. The first modern business partner write was compared with a result frozen from the legacy application.

The fixed measurement report covers 30 merged modernization pull requests and 102,587.72 reconstructed Copilot credits through the first accepted portable demo. The credit total is not a dollar cost. More important, the report says exactly what the result was not: it was not a claim that every ADempiere screen or production deployment had been modernized.

I stopped because the proof-of-concept question had been answered. The result demonstrated a build on the selected runtime, old and new paths running together, and a real business write checked against the legacy result. Completing the rest would have required a product funding decision, not another technical proof. Stopping at that boundary was part of the method.

After repeating this work, I didn’t want the evidence checklist and decision rules to live only in my notes. I encoded them in the public doc-and-modernize agent skill.

Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when a task is relevant. A project skill can live with one repository:

Only SKILL.md is required; the resource folders shown here are optional. The file needs YAML frontmatter with a name and a description explaining what the skill does and when to use it, followed by the instructions. The creation guide includes the full format.

Paraphrased from the commit-pinned skill source, its decision fork is:

The full skill adds the feasibility check, testability milestone, safety levels, phase gates, and evidence requirements.

The useful distinction is procedure versus policy. A shared skill can require repository evidence, bounded experiments, explicit safety levels, and runnable exit criteria. Your organization still needs to supply the parts only it knows:

The skill should make those decisions visible. It shouldn’t make them for you.

Choose an application with an identified owner, known business value, and one workflow you can observe. Run the documentation workflow first. Review the architecture, commands, runtime surfaces, and unknowns with the people who own the system.

Then approve one experiment, not a portfolio rewrite.

Inspect the skill and its supporting files before adding it to a project. GitHub CLI’s gh skill commands are in public preview; check the current installation guidance when you’re ready to use them.

Explore the doc-and-modernize agent skill >

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

#9842. The security of US water systems is even leakier than we thought

And intruders don't always need to exploit bugs to break in

American water systems are even less secure than we thought, according to a study of 236 technology vendors that provide gear to US drinking water, wastewater, and industrial water systems.

The federal government has issued 4,014 security advisories for industrial control systems and cataloged 1,792 vulnerabilities known to have been exploited in cyberattacks. A new index, called Water Supply Chain Watch and published by exposure management firm Securin, however, found almost twice as many vulnerabilities as public records identified – including 20 exploited flaws that weren't even in the federal government's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The security provider compared data on water-tech vendors with records from the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the FBI, and WaterISAC, drawing on CISA advisory data through November 20 and KEV catalog entries through November 23.

It found that federal water advisories hit their highest level this year since 2020.

However, the volume of security alerts isn't a reliable predictor of real-world attacks, the researchers noted.

Five vendors – Rockwell Automation (58), Advantech (48), Schneider Electric (35), Siemens (26), and ABB (24) – account for 191 of the 376 water-tagged security advisories. The No. 2 firm, Advantech, accounted for the highest number of vulnerabilities rated critical, but none of the CVEs in its advisories appear in CISA's KEV catalog. Unitronics, on the other hand, accounted for only two water-tagged security advisories, but at least 75 of its controllers were compromised between November 2023 and January 2024 by attackers taking advantage of default or missing passwords.

The report also highlights another disconnect between water-related CVEs and real-world cyberattacks, which don't always require attackers to exploit software bugs. The July intrusions, which security researchers suspect were the work of Iran-linked attackers, targeted more than 100 water systems, with incidents reported across at least 12 states, and involved poorly secured internet-connected controllers.

According to Securin, 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers across multiple industries in the US were exposed to the internet as of November 17.

Additionally, research by Forescout cited by the security shop found that most exposed Rockwell controllers in the US – seven in 10 – sit on mobile carrier networks, where poorly secured cellular modems can provide an entry point for attackers. A CISA advisory from July describes this technique:

The authoring agencies observed Iranian-affiliated APT actors using several foreign-based IP addresses to access internet-facing PLCs manufactured by Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley, Schneider Electric, Siemens, and potentially other manufactured PLCs [T0883]. The actors used leased, third-party hosted infrastructure and manufacturers’ PLC programming software to connect to misconfigured victim PLCs. Inbound malicious traffic has been observed targeting PLC devices on the following ports: 44818, 2222, 102, and 502, as well as targeting modems on port 22.

These cellular modems, often installed by third-party contractors, frequently aren’t documented.

Unsurprisingly, the top recommendation for water utilities is to find every cellular modem in the environment, including those installed by contractors, make sure they aren’t exposed to the open internet, and put a gateway with multifactor authentication (MFA) in front of them to stop would-be intruders from gaining access via the modem and controller combo.

“Water utilities are spending time and money fixing the vulnerabilities they're told to worry about,” Securin CEO Srinivas Mukkamala said in a statement. “Meanwhile, attackers are getting in through equipment nobody knew was connected or passwords nobody bothered to change.” ®

#9839. The sky was once full of stars, kids; then the FCC let Elon Musk launch a million datacenter satellites

Approval for ‘Starmind’ granted but it’s a long way from the launchpad, or making sense

The United States Federal Communications Commission has approved SpaceX’s plan to launch a million datacenter satellites.

The regulator on Wednesday published an order [PDF] allowing SpaceX to operate a “Non-geostationary satellite orbit (NGSO) constellation of 1,000,000 satellites deployed into orbital shells each spanning 50 km at altitudes from 500 to 1,002 km and in 30-degree inclinations and sun-synchronous inclinations.”

The order requires SpaceX to ensure its satellites’ radios don’t interfere with US government systems which use the 28.6-29.1 GHz band and requires the company to stick to operating within the parameters it files with the International Telecommunications Union.

SpaceX asked the FCC to waive its rule requiring the atmospheric disposal of dead satellites orbiting at 2,000 km or less.

Elon Musk’s company asked for “flexibility to dispose satellites operating above 600 km altitude into Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.”

The FCC found SpaceX did not provide enough information to let it assess if proposed “alternative disposal methods” are compliant with regulations, so deferred its decision on the waiver request.

“SpaceX must file an application for modification of this authorization and provide sufficient justification for any requested waiver(s) of the Commission’s rules,” the order states. The company must also file twice-yearly reports about “conjunction events” – moments when its satellites get dangerously close to each other, or other orbiters.

Whether orbiting datacenters are feasible, make sense, or will ever pay for themselves, remain open questions.

Analyst firm Gartner has described the idea as “peak insanity.”

Google thinks orbiting datacenters become viable if launch costs fall to $200/kg, which would mean SpaceX needs to launch its massive Starship 1,800 times. SpaceX’s assumptions assume near-daily launches, far better than its current cadence of a launch every three days or so.

Fundamental networking research must also come to fruition to handle the amount of traffic large constellations of orbiting datacenters will create.

Terrestrial manufacturing capacity will also need to increase to build all those satellites. Elon Musk’s companies and Intel have planned a giant new fab to make that possible, without explaining how the supply chains behind chip manufacturing will scale to make it feasible. That's a notable omission given that semiconductor supply chains are already extremely strained.

Approval for SpaceX is therefore nice but in no way a roadmap to a million datacenter satellites.

Google, ironically, is a little further along than SpaceX, having launched a test sat in October and last week announcing it has hired Amazon founder Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to launch a larger satellite carrying the equivalent of a full datacenter rack in early 2029.

Down on Earth, meanwhile, scientists trying to observe the universe continue to bemoan the obstructions caused by mega-constellations of broadband-beaming satellites. Proposals from across the USA, China, Europe and India currently call for around 100,000 satellites. SpaceX’s proposed million orbiters could run workloads which help us to understand the mysteries of the universe while also making them hard to see from down here. ®

Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here’s what we can learn through that process as developers.

As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.

In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!

For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward, VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.

The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.

Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!! #GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5

you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge! repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY

According to the Octoverse report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.

With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!

AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.

As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.

What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!

At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.

Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.

AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.

In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.

It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a lot to the maintenance burden.

Efforts need to be made by all of us, like the one shared here, to help ease burdens for maintainers.

As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”

Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:

Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.

We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does. Give it a go on our virtual badge, and try tinkering on it yourself.

Then get your hands on your own badge. We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

#9832. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:'God Mode' Flaws Could Wreak Border-Control Havoc

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

#9831. From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

When selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

The launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

#9830. India’s government ponders cradle to grave AI oversight

Machines of loving grace to turn social media grumps into services, finger painting into career advice

Indian politicians have proposed that AI could take a major role in citizens’ lives, partly through pervasive surveillance.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi last week spelled out his vision for an AI-based app that would collect data about children as they grow and analyze it to determine their aptitude for different types of study or careers.

Modi suggested that parents of three-year-old children should enter data about their offspring’s activities and accomplishments into a government-run system that is also accessible to teachers and even a child’s friends. Those records, the PM suggested, will “help identify children's interests and aptitude from an early age and redirect them in the study of their choice in future.”

That’s not an entirely creepy idea, because gaining access to India’s top tertiary institutions requires students to pay a hefty fee to sit for entrance exams. Modi pitched recommendations from the AI-powered app as something parents will appreciate as they contemplate whether to fund their offspring’s studies.

India’s most populous state, Uttar Pradesh (UP), has proposed to build an “AI Stack” to serve its 240 million-plus residents.

A 178-page tender seeks bidders to build a system that uses the state’s Family ID – a unique identifier for each household – to link data held by multiple agencies so it can be put to work in a dozen AI use cases.

One of those use cases is a tool for “AI-Enabled Social Media Monitoring and Urban Grievance Detection” that “analyses publicly available social media content including online news channels and connected grievance channels to detect emerging urban issues, citizen complaints, service interruptions, and recurring service gaps.”

The government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps.

Another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits.

Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes.

UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets.

India’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention important oversight measures for the AI Stack. ®
